# Baylor Athletics Technology Inventory Analysis

On 2026-08-30, the Baylor Athletics Technology Inventory project (`~/DEV/Tech_Inventory_Analysis`) was finalized for distribution: a web report was published, a PDF rendered, a `.docx` added, and all deliverables copied to OneDrive under `00_Primary_Storage_Drive/05_SYSTEMS/SoftwareTechDocs/TechInventory_2026-08/`. The session's most consequential outcome was not a deliverable but a correction — searching meeting transcripts revealed the survey was still open, forcing all four documents to be reframed as an **interim** read rather than a closed finding. A 2026-09-07 verification pass confirmed the data had not moved and surfaced a platform-documentation mismatch that would have produced a false "no new responses" answer.

## Key Points

- **The survey is not closed.** 29 August was Applied Performance's *internal* deadline; the 24 August all-staff meeting set a **department-wide soft deadline of 29 September**. Five non-responding units (27 of 33 in) are outstanding, not delinquent — the original wording read as blame.
- **As of 2026-09-07 nothing had changed:** 37 response rows, still 27 of 33 units, newest source still `raw/Quick_Inventory_export_2026-08-29.xlsx`, byte-identical by md5 to the OneDrive copy, no newer export anywhere in the home folder. The five outstanding units are Golf (M), Tennis (M), Tennis (W), Volleyball, and Business Office; "Other" is a catch-all box, not a real department.
- **The live survey runs on Microsoft Forms, but project docs point at Google Forms** from the 08-13 proposal era — a trap that would make a `gws` query return a truthful-but-false empty result. See [[concepts/microsoft-forms-vs-google-forms-inventory-mismatch]].
- **Deliverable format was determined from transcripts, not guessed.** Kenny's own words from the 13 August meeting — "the more simple and concise, almost like **one page checklist**" and "I do think we need to figure out all the systems that we're using" — plus Jon Allen's "nobody knows everything that exists" (80–90% known) support building a one-page executive summary matching the existing `Software_and_Tech_Management_EXEC_SUMMARY_ER_2026-08-14.docx` pattern, with the 10-page report retained as the working document.
- **PII discipline on publication:** `raw/*.xlsx` contains respondent names and email addresses and was neither published nor copied; the PDF, HTML, and docx were scanned to confirm no PII before distribution. `README.md` (script run instructions) was deliberately withheld, available on request.
- **Copy, not move, to OneDrive.** Deliverables were placed next to the existing Software and Technology Management framework docs using the established `_ER_<date>` filename convention; local originals were left untouched.
- **Docx tables are generated from the clean CSVs** (`uv run --with python-docx python3 scripts/build_docx.py`) so prose and data cannot drift — a guard that was needed, since hand-written prose in the same docx said "roughly thirteen vendors" while listing twelve (Switch missing).
- **Data resolutions:** "Marketing and Fan Experience" merged into Marketing (34 → 33 units, Marketing no longer a gap); Red Card identified as the athlete meal-money stipend, holding athlete identity/spending data (athlete-data count 59 → 60). Two of 324 product names — **SCRL app** and **JABA** — remain unidentified.

## Details

The framing error is the session's central lesson and generalizes well beyond this project. The analysis had been written as though the response window had closed, which turns five missing units into an implicit accusation of non-compliance. The actual governance timeline — an internal Applied Performance deadline of 29 August nested inside a department-wide soft deadline of 29 September — was recoverable only from meeting transcripts, not from the survey artifact itself. This is the same discipline applied to the deliverable-format question: rather than infer what Kenny would want from a report, the transcripts were searched for his stated preference, which turned out to be an explicit "one page checklist." In both cases the authoritative record lived in a channel outside the working artifact, and consulting it changed the output materially. The Fireflies transcript corpus functions here as a governance source of truth, the same role it plays in [[concepts/athletics-performance-landing-page-spec]], where a spec was grounded in a specific meeting rather than assembled from assumption. A parallel language edit followed the same source: "nothing in the current process notices this" was reworked into forward-looking capability language to match Kenny's known review preferences.

The 2026-09-07 resume session shows what maintaining an interim deliverable actually costs. The question "has anything changed?" was answered by going to the raw `.xlsx` rather than the cleaned CSV, comparing the local and OneDrive copies by md5 rather than by filename, and searching the whole home folder for a newer export — three independent checks to establish a negative. That thoroughness paid for itself by exposing the Microsoft-Forms-versus-Google-Forms documentation drift, which is invisible downstream of the cleaning step and would otherwise have been discovered only after a future session trusted a stale form ID. The practical consequence is that this project's refresh loop is human-gated: the export cannot be pulled from any CLI, so the interim label persists until someone manually downloads a new file and runs `uv run --with openpyxl python3 scripts/clean_inventory.py`, confirming `clean/unmapped_review.csv` is empty.

The generation-hygiene findings echo failures catalogued elsewhere in this knowledge base. Headless Chrome stamped a `file:///Users/...` path into the PDF footer by default and a page-break rule left a half-empty page — neither of which is detectable from the output's byte size, only from inspecting the rendered PDF, the same render-layer verification rule established in [[connections/verify-before-trusting-tool-output]] and exercised on Excel conditional formatting in [[concepts/openpyxl-conditional-formatting-alpha-gotcha]]. The prose/data drift ("roughly thirteen vendors" over a list of twelve) is the specific failure that generating tables directly from CSVs is meant to prevent; that the drift survived in the hand-written surrounding prose shows the guard covers only the generated region, and hand-written summary sentences over generated data remain a live drift surface. Because every document rebuilds from the pipeline, the post-29-September plan is mechanical: re-export the survey data, re-run the pipeline, and all four documents regenerate with final numbers — which is also why the one-page executive summary can be built now (marked interim) at negligible cost.

# Native Windows Python Cannot Open a Git Bash /tmp Path

A document-extraction script written during the 2026-10-04 Digest build failed because it wrote output to a Git Bash `/tmp` path. Git Bash presents a POSIX-style filesystem rooted in its MSYS installation, but a native Windows Python interpreter does not participate in that translation: it resolves `/tmp/...` against the current drive root, producing a path like `C:\tmp\...` that does not exist. The fix recorded in the repo's STATUS Gotchas section was to anchor output relative to the script's own directory rather than to an absolute POSIX path.

## Key Points

- **The POSIX root is a Git Bash illusion, not a system fact.** MSYS translates paths for processes it launches through its own layer; a native Windows interpreter sees the literal string.
- **The failure is a confusing one rather than an obvious one.** `/tmp` resolves to a syntactically valid Windows path under the current drive, so the error is "no such directory" rather than "malformed path."
- **The durable fix is relative anchoring.** Deriving the output location from the script's own file location removes the dependency on any shell's notion of a root.
- **This is the same hazard as writing handoffs to `/tmp`** on a Unix host for a different reason — the path resolves somewhere, just not somewhere useful or persistent.
- **Cross-shell scripts should avoid absolute paths in either dialect.** A path that works in Git Bash may fail in PowerShell and vice versa; a script-relative path works in both.

## Details

This belongs to a well-populated family of Windows findings in which a tool's environment assumptions do not survive being handed to a different executor. Claude Code's hooks run through bash even when the interactive shell is PowerShell, so PowerShell-syntax hook commands fail; `setx` writes the registry while running processes keep their launch-time environment; Task Scheduler spawns with a minimal PATH that bare executable names cannot resolve. The common structure is that one layer's conventions — shell syntax, environment snapshot, PATH, filesystem root — are assumed to be universal and are not. Here the assumed-universal convention is the POSIX filesystem root, and the executor that does not share it is `python.exe`.

The practical rule generalizes past this one case. Any absolute path written into a script encodes an assumption about which layer will interpret it, and on a mixed Windows/Git Bash machine that assumption is frequently wrong and always invisible until something runs. Anchoring to the script's own directory removes the assumption entirely rather than replacing it with a better one — the same move as making a synced config reference `$HOME`-relative rather than picking whichever absolute path is correct on the current host. The failure is also cheap to miss during development: a developer who happens to run the script from a shell whose translation layer *does* apply will see it work, and the breakage appears only when the invocation path changes.

# Project Memory Index Size as a Recurring Per-Session Cost

On 2026-09-30 a `doctor-plus` context audit found the project memory index had grown to roughly 8,200 characters — a cost paid at the start of every session, because the index is auto-loaded rather than retrieved on demand. The index was trimmed from 8,162 to 5,549 characters (~30% smaller) by rewriting each line to state only *when to open* the file it points at, leaving all dates, counts, and error text inside the memory files themselves. All 56 links were verified after the rewrite.

## Key Points

- **The index is always-loaded, so its size is a standing tax**, not a one-time storage cost; growth that would be unremarkable in a retrievable file is expensive here.
- **The durable fix is a line-format rule, not a one-off cut:** each index line states only the condition under which a reader should open the target file. Details belong in the target.
- **Trim measured 8,162 → 5,549 chars (~30%)** with no pointer removed — the reduction came entirely from moving content down a tier, not from dropping entries.
- **All 56 links were verified after the rewrite**, because a reformatting pass over a pointer file is exactly the operation most likely to produce a dangling pointer.
- **This is the same lever applied one layer out** from the Tier A index trim (15 → 10 files) and the repeated `MEMORY.md` cap trims, and it has the same failure mode: without a format rule, the file re-grows.

## Details

A pointer index occupies an unusual position in the memory architecture: it is the mechanism by which content becomes retrievable rather than resident, and yet it is itself resident. That makes it the one file where restating a fact is doubly expensive — the fact is paid for in the index every session *and* stored again in the file the index points at. The observed growth to ~8,200 characters came from exactly that duplication: index lines had accumulated dates, counts, and error strings that already existed in their targets, apparently on the reasoning that a richer index saves a read. The trim rejects that trade, because a read is conditional and cheap while the index is unconditional.

Encoding the fix as a line *format* rather than a size target is what distinguishes this pass from the earlier wording-compression attempts on `MEMORY.md` catalogued in [[concepts/memory-cap-relief-by-migration-not-deletion]]. Compression shortens prose and buys bytes that are immediately re-spent; a format rule ("state when to open this file, nothing else") answers the question that produces the growth in the first place, so the next person adding an entry knows what not to write. It also makes the index auditable: a line containing a date or a count is visibly out of format and can be fixed without a judgment call about whether it is worth its bytes. This is the same move as recording a mechanism instead of a magic number in [[connections/document-the-mechanism-not-the-magic-number]] — the abstraction level of the recorded content is chosen to match how stable that content is.

The link verification step matters because a bulk reformat is precisely the operation that silently breaks pointers. Fifty-six links rewritten by hand or by pattern is fifty-six chances to mistype a target, and a broken index entry is worse than a verbose one: a verbose entry costs tokens, while a dangling one resolves to nothing and makes a real memory file invisible. Verifying after the pass rather than trusting the edit is the same discipline as re-running the doctor to confirm a cap fix, and the same hazard as the stale-pointer class described in [[connections/a-stale-pointer-resolves-cleanly-to-the-wrong-answer]].

# Memory Recall Evaluation Harness (30-Question Retrieval Benchmark)

The recall-eval harness is a scheduled benchmark that scores competing memory-retrieval methods against a fixed 30-question set, writing results to `~/.claude/audits/recall-eval/LATEST.md`. On 2026-10-01 a manual run against a freshly built vault index produced the first fully-scoreable comparison of four methods, and its numbers were used to adjudicate whether the Docker/Milvus-backed memsearch stack should be retired in favor of a cheaper alternative. The harness exists precisely so that a retrieval-infrastructure decision is settled by measurement rather than by cost intuition.

## Key Points

- **Four methods, 30 questions (2026-10-01 run):** memsearch 29/30 hit@5, 15 hit@1, 5.7 s; fts5 + Jev 27/30, 19 hit@1, 0.4 s; plain fts5 25/30, 20 hit@1, 5 ms; `rg` 23/30, 11 hit@1, 111 ms. Coverage was 14/14 Tier A notes and 12/13 vault notes.
- **Pre-registered retirement rule:** memsearch is retired only if a cheaper method comes within 1 hit@5. fts5+Jev trails by 2, so the rule did not fire and the Docker/Milvus stack was kept.
- **Recall and ranking diverge.** memsearch wins hit@5 but loses hit@1 (15 vs plain fts5's 20) — it is better at *finding* the right note than at *ranking* it first. A single headline metric would have hidden this.
- **Indexing the vault changed the verdict's availability, not just its value.** Before the overnight index, memsearch was unscoreable; after it (started 22:30, finished 02:49, 259 minutes, 8,302 chunks) it became the best method on recall.
- **The scheduled run failed silently and is not yet diagnosed.** The eval task queued after the index died within ~7 seconds, runs fine by hand, and Task Scheduler history is disabled on the laptop — so the fix is to add output logging to the task before the next Sunday 02:00 run rather than to guess at a cause.

## Details

The harness's value on 2026-10-01 came less from any single score than from the structure it imposed on a decision. The question on the table — keep a Docker/Milvus semantic-search stack or drop to SQLite FTS5 — is exactly the kind of question that gets answered by vibes: the cheaper method is dramatically faster (5 ms versus 5.7 s) and carries no container dependency, and a stopped Milvus container had already caused days of memsearch timeouts (see [[concepts/memsearch-tool-maintenance]]). A pre-registered bar — "within 1 hit@5" — prevented that convenience from deciding the matter. fts5+Jev landed 2 behind, the rule did not fire, and memsearch stayed. This is the same discipline as writing a pass bar before running a model (see [[concepts/pre-registered-pass-bar]]) and the same demand that a model be justified by the failure of the strongest cheap alternative rather than any alternative (see [[connections/measured-baseline-before-model-adoption]]) — here the cheap alternatives were genuinely strong, and the rule was honored in the direction of keeping the expensive tool.

The hit@5 / hit@1 split is the run's most useful substantive finding. Reporting both metrics exposed a behavioral difference the aggregate obscures: memsearch retrieves the relevant note into the top five almost always (29/30) but places it first only half the time (15/30), while plain FTS5 misses more often (25/30) yet ranks precisely when it hits (20/30). Characterized plainly, memsearch is a recall instrument and lexical search is a precision instrument, which argues for using them for different jobs rather than picking one winner. It also means any future retirement test must keep reporting both numbers, since a method that matched memsearch on hit@5 while beating it on hit@1 would be a strict improvement, whereas one that matched on hit@5 alone would be a lateral move.

Two operational lessons attach to the run. First, the overnight index's 259-minute duration confirms that full-library embedding is an hours-scale job belonging to a scheduled task, consistent with the earlier relocation of the heavy reindex into the nightly backup. Second, the eval task's ~7-second death is currently uninformative: it reproduces only under the scheduler, the obvious candidate causes (encoding, a missing API key) were ruled out, and the scheduler's own history is disabled. The chosen response was not a workaround but an instrumentation change — add output logging so the next scheduled failure captures a real error — because an unlogged scheduled job that works by hand supplies no diagnostic surface at all.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. # NCAA Best Practices Doc: Draft v1 Read-Only Verification

On 2026-10-04 Draft v1 of Baylor Athletics' "Performance Technology Best Practices" guide (repo `NCAA_BestPractices_Doc`, commit `a9dabb0`) was verified read-only against its own `docs/GOAL_PROMPT.md` and `docs/PLAN.md`. The pass ran through Codex with no edits and no commits, applied a 10-point check list, and returned a split verdict: **PASS on checks 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9; FAIL on 3 (SSI crosswalk), 6 (internal consistency), and 8 (factual support)**. All 12 deliverables existed and rendered correctly — a 9-page guide plus five 2-page appendices (A–E). A second read-only round the same evening (R2, HEAD `555702d`) adjudicated a third-party audit of that first review, and the day's closeout committed the resulting handoff at `58562b2`. On 2026-10-05 the loop ran two further rounds at the same HEAD — a Codex round-2 pass over Fable's B1–B22 / F1–F7 fix list, and a final R3 ruling on Fable's FINAL FIX LIST — before any fixes were applied.

## Key Points

- **The artifacts were inspected, not regenerated.** PDFs were read with PyMuPDF rather than re-running the build, because `scripts/build_guide.py` drives Word through COM; re-running it would have produced Word-automation side effects during what was meant to be a non-mutating audit. Pagination against the 8–10 page target was therefore left untested through R3, deferred to a later authorized build.
- **The three original failures are all cross-document failures, not formatting ones.** Build artifacts, outline coverage, pending tags, athlete-data hygiene, terminology, and BaylorDoc styling all passed. What failed was agreement between the guide and its appendices, the accuracy of the SSI crosswalk's coverage claims, and whether specific factual assertions had any source pointer at all.
- **Paired athlete-facing and policy documents drifted apart on the same rule.** Guide §4.3's staff access matrix grants Athletic/Applied Performance *flags only* on raw wellness data, while Appendix A's athlete-facing disclosure says Athletic Performance sees wellness check-ins. R2 settled this: Athletic Medicine sees raw wellness responses; Athletic Performance and coaches see flags only. R3 found Section C's wearable-access string had dropped the §4.3 consent exception, while its body-composition string did match.
- **A gate form with an "N/A" option is not a gate.** Appendix B permits N/A on rows 1–6, which the guide states must all be met. R2 resolved this as a tiered rule: OGC approval retained for rows 1–3, with rows 4–6 requiring a recorded reason plus Procurement/OGC review (`forms.py:103`).
- **Crosswalk "Met" statuses overstated coverage in two rows,** and R2 answered the *decides*-vs-*reviews* gap with a documented Level 3 Working Group decision plus delegated Level 2 decisions subject to ratification. R3 then narrowed the quorum question: SSI requires student-athlete participation in *developing and reviewing the plan*, not a seat in every technology vote, so both athlete seats are invited and their input or nonresponse recorded, while a four-seat quorum lets decisions proceed over breaks.
- **The dominant defect class, named in R2 and confirmed across R3, is proposed framework language presented as current practice.** R3 added item 17's "revised with … input," which framed a future review as already done and was replaced with a date-anchored commitment ("By November 6: submit… after OGC, Procurement, ITS and Athletic Medicine input").
- **Fix lists written against rendered prose are not applicable as search strings.** Many of Fable's locators (B1–B3, B5, B10–B11, B17, B22, F5; later items 10 and 13) span adjacent Python string literals in `scripts/build_guide.py`, so the quoted text exists only after rendering — edits must target the containing `d.para` calls, located by section number.
- **Two R3 rulings held the prior reviewer's line against a revision.** The B12 storage cell keeps "Storage location unverified [Pending ITS: approved restricted Baylor-controlled storage]" rather than asserting a location still under ITS review, and F3's vendor-pooling disclosure stays in the Appendix A notice table where an athlete looks for data uses, with a rights bullet permitted only as reinforcement.
- **The page budget was defended against convenience cuts.** The 8–10 page target was kept but the proposed Section D cuts were explicitly *not* pre-authorized: folding §1.3 would hide the review rule and trimming Appendix A's opening would remove consent context.

## Details

The useful structure of the first verification is that every passing check was intrinsic to a single document and every failing check was relational. A pending-tag sweep, a styling check, a terminology check, and an athlete-data hygiene check can each be answered by reading one file. Internal consistency, crosswalk accuracy, and factual support cannot: they require holding two artifacts side by side and asking whether the second is entitled to what it says about the first. This is why a guide can be complete, correctly built, correctly styled, free of placeholder markers, and still be unsafe to publish — the defects live in the seams. The specific seams here were guide-to-appendix (access matrix vs. disclosure; mandatory rows vs. N/A column), guide-to-crosswalk (what the crosswalk claims is "Met" vs. what the cited passages actually say), and guide-to-sources (claims with no pointer, plus one claim whose pointer says something narrower than the guide does).

Two of the findings generalize beyond this document. The first is that *paired documents describing one rule need a single source of truth*: an access matrix in a staff-facing guide and a plain-language disclosure in an athlete-facing appendix are two renderings of the same policy, and maintaining them as independent prose guarantees eventual divergence. The second is attribution precision: Guide §1.4 assigned "unchallengeable, autonomous authority" to Athletic Medicine generally, where the SSI source (`SOURCES.md:63`) assigns it specifically to *primary healthcare providers*. The remedy recorded is not to drop the claim but to restate it with the source's actual subject while keeping Baylor's own Athletic Medicine routing. Three further claims (a seven-unit figure, a nine-retirement figure, and a transfer-history assertion) have no source pointers and were flagged for sourcing rather than removal.

The R2 round added a different kind of value: it adjudicated a prior review rather than re-reading the document from scratch, issuing AGREE / DISAGREE / AGREE-WITH-CHANGE verdicts with `file:line` evidence. It answered open factual questions from primary evidence — the VALD email folder showed only an *intended* two-school transfer workflow, and no local Catapult/VALD/Kinexon contract terms establish that individual exclusion from norm pooling is even available, converting an unconditional individual opt-in into an institution-level prohibition plus athlete notice. It also *rejected* a suggestion (trimming Section 6, on the grounds that page count alone is not reason to delete a risk explanation) and surfaced two findings the first pass missed: the framework routing sheet already routes GPS, load monitoring, and force plates to Level 3, contradicting the guide's level table; and the Data Steward holds unique duties with no named backup. A second Codex pass on 2026-10-05 ran the same adjudication shape over Fable's structured fix list, returning OK on fourteen rows, CHANGE on fourteen, and DROP on none — and answered three procedural questions: follow this guide's routing sheet labelled as a proposed reading pending ITS confirmation; an email decision can satisfy SSI's "decides" provided quorum, deadline, and urgent-request handling are defined (a chair-called email vote closing in ten working days); and Appendix A audiences should be generated from one shared access definition with a deliberate wellness exception. It also performed two fact checks without opening athlete data — confirming DexaProject sits on a Drive attached to a *personal, non-Baylor* account, and that `S2_Evaluation/docs/program/executive-report.md` does appear to contain athlete names — answering yes/no without displaying contents.

The R3 round on 2026-10-05 is the clearest illustration of why a review chain needs a terminal adjudicator rather than more reviewers. Its verdict — "Apply R3_fable.md with these amendments" — accepted one of Fable's positions (quorum, as amended), upheld the prior reviewer against Fable on two (B12 storage wording, F3 placement), and declined to pre-authorize a page-budget trim. It also caught the characteristic side effect of a fix list applied without re-reading the surrounding text: adding a licence sentence to item 13 left §4.4 self-contradictory, with Applied Performance "working with" Athletic Medicine to interpret health data, when interpretation must sit with licensed Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance may only prepare reports under oversight. A second cluster (items 10/21/27/28) showed two fixes pulling in opposite directions on vendor language: "only to run their service" contradicts the permitted de-identified norm pooling while "anyone else outside Baylor" sweeps in contracted vendors, resolved by defining "outside release" as release beyond Baylor's contracted service providers. Three remaining gaps carried out of the round-2 pass — §2.1 still stating that every request *goes through* the unadopted framework, §1.1's consensus/tie rule conflicting with the new email vote, and Appendix A's blanket "not sent outside Baylor" claim conflicting with vendor hosting — together with crosswalk and `OPEN_ITEMS.md` edits adding CUBI / Texas Medical Records Privacy Act applicability, item T4 (ITS routing-sheet confirmation), V1 (vendor exclusion feasibility), and the DexaProject and S2 storage exceptions.

The closeout pass of 2026-10-04 is where the review output became a tracked state rather than a transcript. A handoff note was written to `docs/handoffs/2026-10-04-guide-draft-v1-and-review-loop.md` and committed at `58562b2`, and the repo's `STATUS.md` had to be rewritten because its `## Open questions` section pointed at `PLAN.md` instead of stating the questions — a form invisible to the extractor feeding the next morning's decision list. The surviving dependencies are all external to the repo: a Chris meeting to book by 10/14 with the guide PDF in hand, an ITS answer on the routing sheet and storage location, vendor confirmation on individual pooling exclusion, and two athlete-data placement decisions (DEXA storage, and `Ath_Medicine` / `Catapult_API` / `S2_Evaluation`) that sit with Eric.

# Goal Prompt Pointer Pattern Under a Character Limit

On 2026-10-05 a `/goal` run to produce Draft v1 of Baylor Athletics' "Performance Technology Best Practices" guide hit a 4,000-character limit on the goal text. The resolution was to keep the full brief in a committed repo file — `NCAA_BestPractices_Doc/docs/GOAL_PROMPT.md` — and hand `/goal` a roughly 760-character pointer that still enumerates all seven done-checks, so the goal remains independently judgeable without carrying the brief. The split was committed as `d1fbb7f`.

## Key Points

- **The limit is on the goal field, not on the work.** A brief too long for `/goal` does not need to be shortened; it needs a durable home and a pointer.
- **What must survive compression is the completion criteria, not the instructions.** The pointer kept all seven done-checks verbatim-in-substance because a goal whose success condition is only reachable by opening another file cannot be judged by the harness or by a later reader.
- **The full brief is committed, not transient.** Writing it to `docs/GOAL_PROMPT.md` and committing it makes the originating specification auditable against the delivered artifact — which is precisely what the subsequent read-only verification rounds checked the draft against.
- **Path typos cost a round trip.** `/cd ~/NCAA_BestPractices_Doc` and `~/Destktop/...` both failed before the correct `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\NCAA_BestPractices_Doc` was used.
- **The same session flagged a sequencing risk the prompt could not resolve:** the brief locks in three `PLAN.md` recommendations Chris Ruf has not approved, so running before the 10/14 meeting yields a draft to bring him at the cost of possible rework.

## Details

The pattern generalizes the distinction between a specification and a goal. A specification is long because it must be unambiguous across many decisions; a goal is short because its job is to let an outside observer decide whether the work is finished. Conflating the two produces either a goal too long to fit a field or a goal too thin to evaluate. Splitting them puts each in the place suited to it: the specification in version control where it can be diffed against the output, and the goal in the harness where it drives the Stop hook. The critical design choice is which content crosses into the pointer — here, the done-checks — because that is the only part a judge needs. This is the same reasoning behind the inline-statement requirement for STATUS open questions, where "See PLAN.md" was invisible to the extractor that consumed the field: a machine-readable field cannot hold a pointer its consumer will not dereference, and a `/goal` completion check has the same property.

The commitment of `GOAL_PROMPT.md` turned out to matter more than its role as overflow storage. Every later verification round on this document — the 10-point Codex pass, the R2 adjudication, and the R3 ruling — checked the draft against `docs/GOAL_PROMPT.md` and `docs/PLAN.md` rather than against anyone's recollection of what had been asked for. A brief that had lived only inside a `/goal` invocation would have left those audits with no fixed target, and the "did it do what was asked" question would have degraded into "does this look reasonable." The same session also recorded hard guardrails inside the brief itself (no athlete-identifiable data anywhere including DexaProject and `Injury_Surveillance/data`, staff-facing terminology except when quoting SSI, nothing shared outside Eric, and no marking of Chris's sign-off steps as done in `portfolio.json`), which are only enforceable as review criteria because they are written somewhere a reviewer can read.

# Fix-List Locators Must Anchor on Source, Not Rendered Output

When a document is generated from code, a review conducted on the rendered output produces fix instructions that cannot be mechanically applied. On 2026-10-05 two successive review rounds on the Baylor "Performance Technology Best Practices" guide found that many of the reviewer's locators — B1–B3, B5, B10–B11, B17, B22, F5, and later items 10 and 13 — quoted prose spanning several adjacent Python string literals inside `scripts/build_guide.py`. The quoted text exists only after rendering, so no literal search for it succeeds; edits had to target the containing `d.para` calls, located by section number (§3.3, §4.4) instead.

## Key Points

- **Rendered prose is a join of source fragments.** A sentence that reads continuously in the PDF may be assembled from multiple string literals, so it is not a findable substring of the generator.
- **Ellipses make a quote unusable as a locator.** B18/B19 quoted text with `…` that does not occur anywhere in the file; F3 omitted the real row ending ("to build norms or improve products").
- **Some fix-list entries have no search string at all.** B16 was an insertion, which a search-and-replace framing cannot express.
- **The working locator is structural, not textual:** cite the section number and replace the containing generator call.
- **The prescription for future rounds is to anchor fix lists on literal source fragments** rather than on rendered output — a requirement on the reviewer's output format, not on the applier's cleverness.

## Details

The defect is a mismatch between the layer a reviewer reads and the layer an editor writes. Reading the PDF is correct — it is the artifact that ships, and inspecting it rather than re-running a COM-driven Word build was itself a deliberate choice in this project. But a review whose output is "replace this quoted sentence" silently assumes the quoted sentence is a unit in the source, and in a generated document it usually is not. The result is a fix list that looks precise and executable while roughly a third of its entries cannot be located, which converts a mechanical apply step into a second interpretive pass and introduces exactly the opportunity for drift the fix list was supposed to eliminate.

The remedy has two halves and they belong to different parties. The reviewer must produce locators that exist in the file being edited: a source fragment, a function call, a line range, or a section identifier — anything whose referent is unambiguous in the generator. The applier must treat a rendered quote as a *description* of the target rather than an address for it, resolving it by structure. Stating the rule explicitly ("any future fix list for generated documents should anchor on literal source fragments, not rendered output") is what makes it a reusable convention rather than a per-round workaround, and it is the generated-document instance of the broader pattern that a recorded path or quote decays the moment the layer it names is not the layer being acted on.

# An Applied Fix Can Contradict the Sentence Next to It

A fix list is a set of local edits evaluated individually, which means a correct fix can introduce a new defect in text it does not touch. In the 2026-10-05 R3 review of Baylor's "Performance Technology Best Practices" guide, two such failures were caught before the fixes were applied: adding a licence sentence to item 13 left §4.4 contradicting itself, and four separate items (10, 21, 27, 28) pulled vendor-disclosure language in incompatible directions.

## Key Points

- **The licence fix broke the sentence it was inserted beside.** With the new sentence in place, §4.4 described Applied Performance as "working with" Athletic Medicine to interpret health data; interpretation must sit with licensed Athletic Medicine, with Applied Performance preparing reports under oversight only.
- **Independently-correct edits can be mutually inconsistent.** "Only to run their service" (items 10/21) contradicts the permitted de-identified norm pooling, while "anyone else outside Baylor" (items 27/28) sweeps in contracted vendors who legitimately host the data.
- **The resolution was a definition, not a wording tweak:** "outside release" is defined as release beyond Baylor's contracted service providers, which makes both strings consistent at once.
- **A third instance was an omission rather than a conflict:** Section C's wearable-access string dropped the §4.3 consent exception, while the parallel body-composition string correctly matched the matrix.
- **Catching these required reading the neighbourhood, not the diff.** Each edit is locally valid; only a reviewer holding the surrounding section in view can see the contradiction it creates.

## Details

This is the apply-stage counterpart to the cross-document drift that the earlier verification rounds found. There, two documents rendering the same rule diverged because each was maintained independently; here, two sentences in the same document diverge because each was fixed independently. The common mechanism is that a rule stated in more than one place has no single owner, so any edit touching one statement is implicitly an edit to a distributed claim. A fix list makes this worse by presenting edits as a checklist of discrete items, which invites exactly the item-at-a-time evaluation that cannot see interaction effects. The practical consequence is that reviewing a fix list is not the same operation as reviewing its items: the list must be read as a proposed *joint* change and checked for internal consistency and for consistency with the text it leaves alone.

The vendor-language cluster shows why the correct repair is often a definition rather than a rewording. Both candidate phrasings were attempts to express the same underlying policy — athlete data is not released outside Baylor — and both failed because "outside Baylor" is ambiguous about contracted service providers who hold the data on Baylor's behalf. Any amount of sentence-level tuning leaves the ambiguity intact in whichever sentences were not tuned. Fixing the definition of "outside release" once, and letting every mention inherit it, resolves the whole cluster and prevents the next edit from reintroducing the conflict. That is the same move as generating paired disclosures from one shared access definition rather than maintaining them as parallel prose.

# Participation Requirement vs. a Seat in Every Vote

The 2026-10-05 R3 review of Baylor's "Performance Technology Best Practices" guide resolved a governance question by reading the source requirement narrowly: SSI requires student-athlete participation in *developing and reviewing the plan*, not a seat in every individual technology decision. The adopted procedure invites both athlete seats to each matter, supplies the materials, and records input or nonresponse — while keeping a four-seat quorum so decisions can proceed over academic breaks.

## Key Points

- **The requirement's object is the plan, not each vote.** Participation in developing and reviewing the governing plan is a different obligation from mandatory presence at every decision.
- **Invitation plus a record satisfies participation without creating a veto.** Both athlete seats are invited and given materials; their input *or nonresponse* is recorded, so the obligation is discharged by the process rather than by attendance.
- **A quorum that depends on a hard-to-fill seat stalls the body.** Keeping a four-seat quorum means an unreachable athlete representative over a break does not block the group.
- **The reading had to be taken from the source's wording,** the same discipline that earlier forced a Level 3 group *decision* because SSI says "decides" rather than "reviews."
- **The recorded nonresponse is the auditable artifact.** Without it, an uninvited-versus-invited-but-silent distinction is invisible after the fact.

## Details

Two failure modes bracket this decision, and the procedure is designed to avoid both. Reading the requirement maximally — an athlete seat present and voting on every technology decision — produces a governance body that cannot reach quorum during the exact periods (summer, academic breaks) when vendor and procurement deadlines fall, and so produces either stalled decisions or decisions taken outside the documented process. Reading it minimally — athletes consulted once at plan adoption and never again — fails the requirement's evident purpose and is also hard to defend if challenged. The middle construction keeps the obligation continuous (invite, supply materials, every matter) while keeping the decision mechanism robust (quorum does not depend on the seat), and it makes the discharge of the obligation checkable by recording what happened rather than asserting that it was honored.

This is the same move the earlier adjudication round made in the opposite direction. There, the guide had softened SSI's "decides" into "reviews," and the correct repair was to build the stronger mechanism — a documented Level 3 Working Group decision with delegated, ratifiable Level 2 decisions — rather than weaken the sentence to match what existed. Here, the guide was reaching for a stronger mechanism than the source demands, and the correct repair was to match the source's actual verb and object. The consistent principle is that the governing text's wording specifies what must exist, in both directions, and that the design question is which mechanism satisfies that wording while remaining operable. The companion design detail recorded in the same review chain — a chair-called email vote closing in ten working days, with defined handling of urgent requests — serves the same operability concern, since an email decision was judged capable of satisfying "decides" provided quorum, deadline, and urgency are specified.

# Pending Bracket Instead of an Asserted Location

Twice in the Baylor "Performance Technology Best Practices" review chain, a reviewer proposed filling a storage-location cell with the intended answer, and twice the ruling kept an explicit pending marker instead. The final wording is "Storage location unverified [Pending ITS: approved restricted Baylor-controlled storage]" — because the column states where data *is* kept, and ITS has not yet confirmed the location.

## Key Points

- **The column's semantics decide the wording.** A field that answers "where is this data kept" cannot be filled with where it is expected to be kept once approved.
- **The proposed fill was the likely-correct answer,** which is what makes the error tempting: "restricted Baylor-controlled storage" is the intended destination, not a fabrication.
- **The bracket carries both the gap and its owner.** `[Pending ITS: ...]` records what is unknown, who resolves it, and what the expected resolution is, so the cell is actionable rather than merely blank.
- **The same ruling had already been made once** in the earlier round ("Storage location under review [Pending ITS: ...]"), and was re-affirmed on appeal — the pending state survived two attempts to resolve it on paper.
- **Closing the bracket is a tracked external dependency,** recorded alongside the ITS routing-sheet confirmation as an open item rather than left to the document's next editor.

## Details

This is the narrowest possible instance of the defect class that dominated this document's review: proposed or future-state facts written in the present indicative. "Procurement already requires…" described a role an unadopted framework merely assigns; a VALD transfer was described as completed when the evidence supported only an intended workflow; and here a storage location under ITS review would have been stated as current practice. What makes the storage cell instructive is that it is a single table cell with no prose around it, so there is no room for hedging language — the choice is between asserting a location and marking the field unresolved. Choosing the marker makes the document's uncertainty legible at exactly the place a reader would otherwise form a false belief, which is the same reasoning behind leaving blanks visible in a status report rather than reporting a fraction.

The appeal history matters as much as the outcome. A pending bracket is under constant pressure to be closed, because an unresolved field looks like incompleteness and resolving it on paper costs nothing and makes the artifact look finished. The R3 ruling's "KEEP CODEX" verdict is a refusal to trade a real unknown for the appearance of completeness, and it pairs with the same round's refusal to pre-authorize page cuts that would have hidden a review rule and removed consent context. In both cases the reviewer declined an edit that improved the document's surface at the cost of its accuracy, and in both cases the governing question was what a reader would believe after the change.

# Same Daily Log Written on Both Machines: Keep Both Sides

The 2026-10-05 Mac `/closeout` hit a merge on the day's `global-memory` daily log file because the Windows laptop and the Mac had both written to it. The recorded resolution is to keep both versions rather than take either side: the file is an append-only accumulation of session entries, so a union loses no lines. The same closeout committed the deletion of 11 `~/.claude` session logs older than 30 days and kept the `portfolio.json` board edits as a separate data commit.

## Key Points

- **An append-only log conflicts as a union, not a choice.** Both sides hold real entries, so "mine" or "theirs" discards work while keeping both loses nothing.
- **This is the expected outcome, not an incident.** The stated rule is to *expect* a merge on the shared daily log whenever both machines are active on the same date.
- **Deleting the 30-day-old session logs was safe for two independent reasons:** Claude Code prunes them itself, and git history still holds them.
- **Board data was committed on its own.** `portfolio.json` edits went in as a data commit separate from the code commits, keeping per-commit intent clean.
- **Drift is reported at closeout, not repaired.** `portfolio.py crosswalk` flagged 17 items (3 rows pointing at moved folders, 3 Drive folders with no row); none originated today, so none were fixed.

## Details

The resolution follows directly from the file's kind, which is the general principle for cross-machine conflicts: the correct verb is set by what the artifact *is*, and no blanket policy is safe. A revision-style document supersedes, so newest-wins or a real merge applies. A router index is a set keyed by identity, so duplicate entries deduplicate. A daily log is an accumulation of independent records, so both sides' lines are kept. Applying a "Mac wins" default here would have silently dropped a machine's entire day of captured sessions — the same shape as the earlier near-miss where a newest-wins resolution would have discarded 324 unique forecast-log rows. Naming the expectation ("when both machines write the same daily log on the same day, expect a merge on that file") converts a recurring surprise into a known step.

The two surrounding closeout decisions illustrate complementary disciplines. The session-log deletion was justified by two independent recovery paths rather than one, which is what makes a deletion commit defensible without a snapshot. And the choice to report rather than repair the 17 crosswalk drift items keeps closeout bounded to the session's own surface: none of the drift was created today, so fixing it would mean taking on unrelated work at the moment of handoff, and the carried-forward items — the two pre-existing `test_crosswalk.py` failures named as Project_Triage's next step, the stashed extra dcg hook awaiting Windows confirmation, the `USER.md`/`MEMORY.md` caps at 99%, the 2026-11-02 `~/DEV_archive_hold` deletion, and Ask_The_Library's unnamed next step — are recorded as future work instead.

# Connection: Review Chains Need a Terminal Adjudicator

## The Connection

The Baylor best-practices guide accumulated four review rounds in two days — an initial 10-point Codex pass, an R2 adjudication of a third-party audit of that pass, a round-2 Codex verdict on a structured B/F fix list, and an R3 ruling on a FINAL FIX LIST. Each round after the first reviewed a *review* rather than the document. That structure only terminates because the last round's output is a ruling: "Apply R3_fable.md with these amendments," with per-item ACCEPT / KEEP / DISAGREE verdicts and an explicit refusal to pre-authorize certain changes.

## Key Insight

Adding reviewers improves coverage but does not converge. Two independently-framed reviewers produce two fix lists, and a third produces a third; without someone empowered to *rule*, the chain either applies the most recent list (losing earlier findings) or applies all of them (producing contradictions). The R3 round demonstrates both halves of the adjudicator's job: it upheld the earlier reviewer against the newer one twice — keeping the B12 pending bracket and keeping F3's disclosure in the Appendix A notice table — and it caught two defects created *by the fix list itself*, where item 13's licence sentence left §4.4 self-contradictory and items 10/21 conflicted with items 27/28 on vendor language. Neither of those is visible to a reviewer reading the document; both are visible only to one reading the proposed changes as a joint edit.

The second insight is that an adjudicator must be willing to decline. R2 rejected a Section 6 trim on the grounds that page count is not a reason to delete a risk explanation; R3 kept the 8–10 page target but refused to pre-authorize the proposed Section D cuts, because folding §1.3 would hide the review rule and trimming Appendix A's opening would remove consent context. A round that only ever ratifies is not an adjudication layer — it is another reviewer, and the chain has no terminus.

## Evidence

- R3 verdicts (2026-10-05): ACCEPT FABLE (amended) on quorum, KEEP CODEX on the B12 storage cell, KEEP CODEX on F3's placement, and page budget retained with Section D cuts not pre-authorized.
- R3 caught two fix-list-generated defects: the item-13 licence sentence contradicting §4.4's assignment of health-data interpretation, and the items 10/21 vs. 27/28 vendor-language conflict resolved by defining "outside release."
- Round-2 Codex (2026-10-05) returned OK on fourteen rows, CHANGE on fourteen, DROP on none — a per-item ruling shape rather than a fresh finding list.
- R2 (2026-10-04) rejected the Section 6 trim and surfaced two findings the first pass missed, showing an adjudication round can still add findings without becoming a re-review.
- Earlier precedent: a rate-limit-forced switch from Codex to Claude found the plan's biggest error, and a prior approval was judged stale after an amendment that itself contained five new bugs — the same observation that a differently-framed pass over a *changed* artifact is a distinct operation from a pass over the original.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_scrape
entries.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. A named browser profile loads saved session data without saving changes to it.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

profile.description: Loads a saved browser profile without saving changes to it.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_search
entries.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, `developer`, or `gov`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

For a legal or regulatory question, `categories: ["gov"]` returns results in `data.web` with `category: "gov"` and cannot be combined with other categories; `firecrawl_gov_search` is the dedicated tool. Verify gov results' issuer, jurisdiction, status, and version before citing current law.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

objective.description: Optional broader goal for this search, if known. Avoid sensitive information.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation; `gov` searches the Government Index of US federal, state, and local legal and regulatory sources, the index behind firecrawl_gov_search, and cannot be combined with other categories; gov hits can include historical versions, bill text, agency guidance, and third-party reproductions, so verify the issuer, jurisdiction, enacted/effective status, and version before citing current governing law, clarify a missing jurisdiction or ambiguous as-of date, and use general search for non-US questions or missing coverage (no hits does not establish that no applicable law exists). `developer` and `gov` return hits in `data.web` with `category` set to their name; the other categories also filter `data.web`.
